title: Electrician to Astronaut
credit: NASA · Houston We Have a Podcast · public domain

segments.text: Houston, we have a podcast.
Welcome to the official podcast of the NASA Johnson Space Center, episode 327, Electrician to Astronaut.
I'm Leah Cheshire, and I will be your host today.
On this podcast, we bring in the experts, scientists, engineers, and astronauts, all to let you know what's going on in the world of human spaceflight.
Tracy C.
Dyson was selected by NASA as an astronaut candidate in 1998.
As a PhD in chemistry with an impressive research background into the Earth's atmosphere and now a NASA astronaut, Tracy is looking forward to her third
mission to the International Space Station.
Born in Arcadia, California, Dyson earned a bachelor of science degree in chemistry from California State University Fullerton in 1993 and a PhD in chemistry from
the University of California Davis in 1997.
Prior to joining NASA, Dyson designed, constructed, and implemented electronics and hardware associated with the study of atmospheric gas phase chemistry and has developed and presented
numerous papers on methods of chemical ionization for the spectral interpretation of trace compounds.
At the time of her selection in 1998, she was completing her postdoctoral fellowship in environmental science to study atmospheric chemistry at the University of California
Irvine.
Dyson is set to fly on the Soyuz MS-25 mission to the International Space Station for a six-month mission, launching from the Baikonur Cosmodrome Launch Site
31 in Kazakhstan.
She'll be joined by Roscosmos cosmonaut Oleg Novitskiy and spaceflight participant Marina Valiscavaya of Belarus, both of who will spend approximately 12 days aboard the orbital
complex.
This will be Dyson's third flight assignment of her astronaut career and she's scheduled to launch in March 2024.
Now that you have just a glimpse into the wealth of experiences of Tracy Dyson, enjoy this chat with the seasoned astronaut herself.
Tracy, I am so excited that you're here today.
Thank you so much for joining me on Houston.
We have a podcast.
Thank you, Leah.
I'm super excited to be here.
So we'll start off in the beginning,
your background.
Let's talk about life when you were growing up.
You were born in Arcadia, California.
Yes.
Did you stay there for long?
No, no, that was an area where my parents grew up,
went to school, but I grew up all around Southern California in different areas.
And as our, my dad's company grew and our income grew, then the neighborhoods became a little nicer.
So I grew up all around Southern California.
So there are some NASA centers in California.
Did you ever make a pit stop?
Did you ever get to visit when you were a kid?
I didn't.
I hate to admit that,
but I led a much different life growing up than I do now surrounded by all things space.
The closest I got to, you know, space agencies and talk of space was when I'd go out to the high deserts of Southern California and
ride motorcycles.
And I'd lay on my trailer and look up at the vast amount of stars in the dark sky.
And that was my space center.
Wow.
That's really amazing.
We're losing those dark sky spaces.
So I think that's a really sweet memory.
I know something really important in your childhood and then even into now is working with your dad
in his electrical company.
Can you walk me through how that started?
Can you tell me, you know, how that has kind of shaped your path today?
Yeah, I, the problem is I don't know when to stop talking about it.
Cause the more, the older I get, the more experienced I get doing this work, the more I realized just what a foundation that provided for
me.
Both my parents, the fact my mother allowed me to go on a job site when I was a wee little girl, she had a lot
of courage and trust in my dad.
And plus my dad taking on a high energy little girl on the, on a job site with him.
I just commend both my parents, but my dad recognized early on that I was, had like an aptitude and I enjoyed what he was doing
and I had energy.
So he put me to work.
So I was about seven years old.
My earliest memory is being seven years old when I was actually put to work.
I'd gone to job sites with my dad before then, just playing around with my, my, my toys and my roller skates and running around like
a, like a troublemaker.
But then dad started giving me jobs to do.
And I started out with simple hand tools.
I would strip wire and make up receptacles.
And then the more,
the better I got at that, dad would have me climb in ladders cause I wasn't afraid of heights.
And so
I was installing lights.
And then I started wiring up panels and pulling wire and doing all sorts of work.
And I was about 15, 16 years old when my dad started letting me go, cause I could drive.
And so I could go on service calls.
So folks would have problems with their office buildings or their stores and they'd need an electrician.
They'd call us.
And dad was busy either running the company or
overseeing a job with the rest of the electricians.
So he could send me out on a service call.
So I'd go and find out what their problem was and, and do what I could to fix it.
And continued on like that, working for my dad, even on the job sites, but also working service calls.
That's impressive.
So you did this, you know, through high school too.
But you also played sports, right?
Yes.
How did you balance that?
That's a really busy schedule.
Right.
Right.
So, um, I, luckily I've had such supportive parents.
So, um, and construct the way construction works, um, I worked for my father for, um, all of my holidays, all of my weekends, um, that
I wasn't engaged in sports and I was, um, in sports all year round, but, um, track primarily.
And so, um, those are weekend meets, but, um, any kind of vacation that I had in summer breaks, I worked for my dad, but, um,
but also construction, you bid a job, you do a job, and then you wait for a little while for another job to come.
And so my dad was, and both my parents were pretty involved in my sports as well.
So yeah, it was a busy life, but I think you need that when you got a lot of energy to keep yourself from getting in
trouble.
I agree.
I agree.
Uh, what'd you run in track?
I was a sprinter and a long jumper.
Impressive.
Yeah.
And you did that in college too, right?
I did.
I, um, all, um, all four years, um, that I could, um, I competed in, uh, track and field.
So it was kind of my, my gig to run fast.
Do you still run?
No, um, I try, but, uh, um, I don't run, but if I did run, um, I'm more of a, I like to say I run
meters, not miles.
And so, um, I like to sprint still.
And I got two, um, energetic dogs, uh, Rhodesian ridge backs, and they like to sprint.
So I get my little bursts out, um, with them, but I wouldn't say that I'm quite as routine as I used to be.
I love it.
Um, so you, you mentioned college and I found it really interesting that you did all of this electrical work growing up and then you chose
chemistry in college.
I know.
I, I didn't see it coming either.
Um, but, uh, when I was in high school, there was a teacher, um, his name was Mr.
Smith.
I'll never forget him.
Um, I took chemistry from him and I just loved it because it answered all of the questions that I had growing up, like, why is
the sky blue?
And I really wanted to know.
I mean, I wasn't just asking and, uh, chemistry answered that and, you know, why does water boil?
Chemistry answers that.
And so I think it was then that I started to, um, get, uh, uh, kind of motivated to learn more about chemistry.
I'm just going to read off some of what is in your bio.
Okay.
You studied atmospherically relevant gas phase chemistry by designing and building a laser ionization time of flight mass spectrometer.
What does that mean to the person who has never,
who did not study chemistry?
Yeah, I, um, you know, that work that you just, uh, described
is a combination of my construction skills, as well as my, uh, my love of chemistry.
Um, I think when you love something, you, you are so, um, motivated to understand it that you really plow through the parts that you don't
understand.
And I think it breaks down your barrier of, of ego
and, and forces you to ask questions.
So if there's any success that I've had in life, it's because I've had to, um, I've had to, um, expose my ignorance and ask questions.
And that's exactly what I did.
So all of that stuff that I did in undergrad and graduate school with chemistry, um, building and designing components and using it to, um, get
into the, into the molecular level of, uh, reactions to see what's going on at a level that, that you need special detectors to understand, uh,
just really, uh, catered to my inquisitive, uh, uh, though ignorant mind that wanted to understand more and my love for tools and, and putting things
together and, and solving problems.
It was just a really great combination for me.
So these all seem to build on the subject of atmospheric chemistry.
That was your, uh, postdoc, correct?
Yes.
Yeah, thanks.
Um, that was where I worked for, um, Barbara Finlayson-Pitts, who is, uh, she's the queen of atmospheric chemistry.
So I was really blessed to have somebody as, um, knowledgeable and experienced as she guiding me through this project.
Um, and I got to use a lot of my skills that I came from, um, my graduate career, which is in mass spectrometry and lasers
and, um, ultra high vacuum systems.
And so I got to apply some of that knowledge, um, as well as some pretty, uh, sophisticated, um, chemistry techniques using natural isotopes and things
like that, that, um, have, um, such a beautiful story to tell in, uh, harmonics and, um, just the, the way nature follows, uh, a harmony
that you wouldn't know unless you, um, unless you interrogated it this way.
And so, um, it just really combined a lot of, uh,
fascinations that I had.
Um, I think I'm just rambling now, but I'm in a reverie.
I'm, I'm in, I'm in awe.
This is, it's amazing.
Um, so that's, is that why you chose atmospheric chemistry?
You know, did something always point you to that specific field?
I think, I think actually living in Southern California, atmospheric chemistry is, um, a big deal because of the location, um, and, and in Southern California,
where I was, we're in a basin.
And so smog was a big deal.
Like I grew up with, um, with smog alerts, like where some kids in the North have to stay home from school because of storms and
snow.
We had to stay home because the smog was too bad.
And so, um, I'd like to, to paint a, a better picture, but it was really because there's a lot of smog in Southern California that
people were wanting to fix this problem.
And so I happened to gravitate towards solving problems, uh, of an atmospheric nature.
Plus, um, once I realized what a vacuum was, more than just that thing that you drag on the floor and pick up particles, like it
is like the vacuum of space, what that really means and what, um, what molecules do in a vacuum just blew my mind.
And, um, the more I understood that, the more interesting chemistry became to me.
So yeah, I kind of gravitated to it, but I think it was all location because it was a problem that, that, that state was willing
to, to tackle.
Wow.
Yeah.
I did all of my education in California.
So it, it was sort of like, what else would you study about chemistry?
So with all of this buildup, was astronaut in mind at any point during this?
You know, the whole astronaut thing was sort of a, like, I didn't know how I was going to get there.
I wanted to be an astronaut and, um, people, when they'd asked me what I wanted to be, and when I realized that's what it was,
I was about 16.
And so I would, and I talk about it, like real serious, like I'm going to, I want to be an astronaut.
And there's some people who would, who would embrace that and ask me like real serious questions.
And there were some who were skeptical, of course, like that's, you know, no one, no one ever makes, you know, that.
Um, and then I'd get people telling me what I needed to do in order to become an astronaut.
And some of that involved going into the military and things that, that, um, I were not on my, my radar.
And, so, um, but somehow I felt like, well, I'll get there, but I'm just going to keep pursuing the things that I enjoy doing.
And, um, I didn't even at the time that I said, I want to be an astronaut, did I think about even getting a PhD?
And it wasn't until I was an undergraduate and I went to a college, Cal State Fullerton is an undergraduate institution, but to their credit, especially
in their science department, they really emphasize undergraduate researchers and research.
And what they did was they prepare undergraduates to go to graduate school.
And because of the preparation, I got there, I hit graduate school in a laboratory.
Like I knew what I was doing.
I didn't just get there and then have to learn how to operate in a laboratory or even run one.
I just knew what I was doing.
And, um, it was my undergraduate research advisor who asked me, so what do you want to, what do you want to do with this degree?
And I'm like, I don't know.
What do I want to do with that?
I just love chemistry.
And, uh, he's like, well, have you thought about graduate?
You want to be an astronaut?
Of course that came out, but he was like, you want to be an astronaut?
So, um, have you thought about getting a PhD?
And I was like, oh, no, no, that's for really smart people.
And he's like, well, you know, you, you gotta be smart, but you just gotta work hard.
And I'm like,
you just gotta work hard?
I mean, I can do that.
And he's like, besides that you get to defer your loans.
And I was like, oh, I'm totally there.
And so, um, he really talked me into it.
Uh, but I, it was the furthest thing from my mind.
And, and then to top it off, once I graduated, um, I remember the day of graduation, I'm, we're standing out there on our caps and
gowns and, um, we're all saying to one another, you know, like, well, so what more can we learn?
I mean, we, we're going to graduate school, but what more can we learn?
We learned everything about chemistry.
And then once we got into graduate school and we had to start teaching chemistry to undergraduates, we realized how much chemistry we really didn't know.
And it was just a good thing that we went on to graduate school.
So, um, anyway, I feel like I'm rambling again, but it just, um, it's so interesting how, um, you know, there's a force in my life,
I'll call it God, that, that guided me on a path that, that was, um, not defined by me.
And if you ask me, like, so you want to be an astronaut, you know, I couldn't tell you that I started out on the right
path, but somehow I ended up, um, in the right place.
And it's been a wonderful journey.
Wow.
So, you know, like you said, you've had this kind of dream since you were 16, when, when NASA, when NASA released that they
were accepting new astronaut applications.
How many times did you apply?
How did you know that it was, this is my chance?
Um, that again was timing.
I applied once and I was in graduate school.
It was, um, the same, so it was in 97 and I applied, um, I, I submitted my dissertation in one month and the following month
I submitted my, um, application to NASA because it turned out that it was, um, just perfect timing for this selection cycle that was coming up.
And I put my application, even though some people said, well, you know, you don't usually get it on your first try.
So I was like, well, I better get it now.
And so I did.
And I even, when I was applying for post-doctoral positions and, um, Dr.
Elizabeth Pitz was interested in having me come work for her, um, I was, and she selected me.
I, I, full disclosure, I said, I just gotta let you know, I submitted my application to NASA for their astronaut program and it's not likely
that I'll get it, but I just feel like I should let you know that before you choose me.
And she was like, okay, well, we'll, we'll take that under consideration and we'll take our chances.
And I was like, okay, we'll take our chances.
And then, and then I got, then I got selected and I had to cut my post-doc short by one year, um, of a two year
post-doc, but I, um, I received a lot of, um, a lot of support from a Dr.
Finlayson Pitz, despite the fact that I had to leave her a year into my postdoc, but yeah, so the first time I applied, uh, I
made it and it was a shock to everybody.
Wow.
Especially me.
But what, what was that call like?
Where were you?
What did it feel like?
I mean, you're shocked, but, but can you explain, can you describe the moment?
Oh yeah, I can relive it over and over.
And I wish that Ken Cockerill was here because he was the, um, chief of the office at the time that I went through my, um,
interview and he remembers as vividly as I do my reaction.
So, um, I actually was at, um, I was at UC Irvine where I was a postdoc and I was in my, in my office.
And at this point, um, in the selection, as you're waiting for the phone call, after everything's been done, you've done all the trips, you've done
all the interviews, you've done all of the medical exams, and now you're waiting for them to make a decision.
Um, you, you kind of anticipating any day now the call's going to happen and it's either going to be, you know, a good news or
it's going to be, um, hey, try again next time.
So, um, I was in my office and I shared an office with a fellow postdoc and we were in, it was a very small office,
so, uh, nobody would have been around to even see my reaction, but the call came and I knew it was a call from outside because
the phone rings a little differently when it's an external call, so already I'm a little bit hyped up because it's, it's not somebody from my
other lab calling me.
No caller ID.
No caller ID.
Oh, yeah, this was way back.
Yeah, you, you, yeah, we use ringers to identify calls, but, um, I picked up the phone and my fellow postdoc was sitting in the desk
behind me, um, so he heard everything, but the voice on the other end was Ken Cockerill and he introduced himself and he said, hi Tracy,
do you remember me?
And I was like, yes, I remember you.
And, and there was also the gouge that if the chief, um, of, of the astro-out office calls you, then that's a very good sign.
So I was trying to keep my composure and he started making like small talk, like chit chat.
And he's like, so how's that truck doing of yours?
I was like, oh, it's doing good.
It's getting by.
And, and, um, he's like, well, you know, the weather out here is, is pretty good about California is excellent.
You, you probably, you know, love living there.
And I'm like, yeah, it's been home and on and on.
And he's like, well, just wanted to know if you're interested in coming to Houston and joining the Astro Corps.
And that's when it started.
I,
my body at that point was shaking and, um, I started to hyperventilate and I didn't know how to answer the phone.
And I know this is a podcast, so you can't see my, my antics over here, but I was,
I was trying to get a hold of my, myself, but I was shaking and I was hyperventilating and I couldn't really answer his question.
He's like, so do you, do you, do you think you might want to come to Houston?
And, and, um, I was still trying to utter a word that sounded legible.
And he said,
I tell you what, how about I call you back in a few more minutes?
That would be good.
And so I hung up the phone and, um, my, my fellow postdoc said, uh, I take it that was NASA.
I said, I made it.
Oh my God, I made it.
And then I busted out the door and I ran all the way up to the fourth floor where the lab and the rest of my
group was and busted through the door.
And I told them, I said, I made it.
I made it.
Oh my God, I made it.
And everybody's jumping up and down and we're high fiving.
And then I was like, oh, wait, the chief's calling back.
I gotta go back.
And so I ran back to my office and, um, caught him just in time.
And so he, um, um, I was able to get my breath and, uh, he gave me a real bad time on the phone for, um,
uh, not being able to talk right away.
And, and then he said, so, um, Tracy, I just needed to let you know one more thing before we get off the phone in 24
hours from now, there'll be a press release that goes out with your name and the rest of your classmates names.
And until then, we'd like you to limit the news to just your immediate family.
And there was the silence that he's like, I take it we're a little late for that.
The science building kind of knows because I went screaming up the stairway.
So it was a long way to answer your question, but it was a very emotional reaction that I had.
Um, I couldn't even control
my shock, I think.
And so, um, it was very memorable.
Wow.
What a story.
And I mean, thank goodness you only had to wait 24 hours before everybody else could know.
Right, right.
So that, yeah, I got in my truck and I drove, I drove, uh, to see the rest of my family and give them the news
in person.
And it was just, it was an amazing day.
Wow.
Yeah.
And that was, uh, you were the 1997 class.
Yes.
Correct.
Okay.
So it was 98, but, but we were selected in 97.
Okay.
Yeah.
We started in 98.
Okay.
So since then, you've had a really impressive career.
Uh, I've, I've been so fortunate, um, to still be here 25 years later.
Um, never saw myself, um, being here this long, but, um, it's been, uh, it's my dream career.
So it's been a real blessing.
When you find it, you've got to keep it.
That's right.
So since then you have worked across several different spacecraft.
Um, you've served as a Capcom for shuttle and space station missions.
And I know that you've had your own shuttle and space station missions.
And then you've also worked on developing the Capcom, or I should define, this is the capsule communicator.
This is a person who speaks with the astronauts, um, when they're either on the space station or when they're in route to the space station.
So you've worked on that for a development of Boeing's Starliner capsule, right?
Yes.
Yeah.
So, um, I, I took that over, um, from Mike Hopkins, who started off as the lead for the, um, the Starliner Capcoms.
And we were a little different in this new commercial crew regime, um, in that, um, Boeing had decided to contract out to NASA the operations
portion of it.
And so, um, there we were developing, uh, the Capcom core for, um, and in, in that development, it's not just what we'll say, but it's,
um, deciding what kind of certifications we need, what type of Capcom.
So there's ascent, there's entry, there's, um, on orbit, there's, um, rendezvous, there's, uh, docking, landing.
And so we had to make decisions about what made sense in terms of, um, when we would, uh, need to be on console and talking
with crew and, and, um, what we had to learn as Capcoms in order to fulfill that mission and support the crew.
And so to talk about the spacecraft that you know best, the ones that you have flown on.
Yeah.
Um, you flew STS-118 in August, 2007.
Yes.
What was that like?
First space flight.
What were your feelings?
What did you work on?
What were you, um, what were your
lessons learned when you came home?
Oh, well, the shuttle, gosh, it was such a, uh, looking back, that was such a unique, um, not only unique timeframe, but, um, the crew
compliment, I mean, you're, you're flying with six other people, seven of us.
And, um, we're in, depending on what we are doing, um, ascent, entry, rendezvous, um, robotics, um, EVA, we're broken into smaller team subsets and, um,
you are with your crew, um, in, um, daily and your crew becomes your, your, your family.
And I mean, like brother, sister, you know, sometimes you're, you're hugging, sometimes you're duking it out as you learn how to work together.
Um, and so you're, and as a rookie, um, I was so, so blessed.
I had, I was on the flight deck with three guys who were not just experienced, but just top-notch at what they did.
And I was so blessed to be the, um, the MS sitting on that, the rookie sitting on the flight deck with those guys on ascent
and rendezvous.
And so I learned so much from those guys, um, just their confidence, their confidence, um, and that they trusted me to, to do the job
I was given, um, in either the ascent or the rendezvous portion of it.
So, um, and then my fellow rookies, uh, um, Barbara and, and Eldrew, we were, um, uh, just so blessed to be on that flight to,
um, uh, dock with the space station and do the kind of, uh, work that we did to, um, uh, transfer elements, um, to help build
the space station.
That was the other part of the shuttle flight that was so unique was every flight was bringing something new to the space station and building
it.
And so you're watching it, um, mission after mission, um, schematic after schematic, uh, the space station was changing on a routine basis.
And so it was really neat to be a part of that and just the newness of being a rookie on a flight that, um,
so historical, um, so meaningful and has played such a role in, um, where we are today.
I look back on that with such fondness that, um, and I'm so, I'm so grateful that I was around to be a part of that.
And both of those flights, your, your first two flights have been to the space station.
So on that first shuttle flight, you were talking about building the space station.
You brought up the S five trust segment, correct?
Yeah, we call it stubby.
Why is that?
Cause the other one's called puny.
Cause you don't really see it.
It's a spacer between the solar array, um, uh, solar array segments.
And so it's very important, but, um, it's, uh, it's not as, um, prevalent when you're looking at those fantastic photos, but yeah, anyway, the S
five, I'm sure you can always pick it out though.
I totally can.
Yeah.
Yeah.
So that was 2007.
You went back in 2010 as part of expedition 23 and 24 on a Soyuz spacecraft.
What was the difference in the space station?
It had only been three years.
That's kind of a short timeframe.
Yeah.
And, um, wow, there seemed like, um, the addition of node three.
So I think node three and the cupola just got there before I arrived on my space station mission from the Soyuz.
Yeah.
So, um, it's a, it's a wonder.
So I, um,
just what comes to mind instantly is that cupola shot that, um, so I was fortunate to be there before we, um, filled the cupola with
a lot of things.
I mean, the, the robotic workstation was there, but, um, in terms of some other equipment that we have in there now, I was able to
nestle myself and put up, uh, cameras and timers and, um, remote devices so I could get that shot.
But, um, I remember being one of the first to, um, to utilize the, the cupola, not just gazing out the window, but actual for robotics
and things like that.
And, um, what, um, what a difference a window or two or seven make.
I mean, it's the shuttle, um, has a great view through the cockpit windows and they are about as large as the windows that are in
the cupola.
Um, but I just couldn't imagine the space station without this cupola.
And, um, it was such a, again, a blessing to have been there at that time to, um, to see not only our beautiful planet and
the space surrounding it, but the space station itself is pretty miraculous.
And it is a sight to behold, whether the sun is up or the sun is down.
It's really cool to see metal coming together in space for the first time and working.
I mean, isn't that amazing that we did that?
It's, I wish more people understood how just magnificent that is.
Right.
And, um, the thousands and thousands of people and the hundreds of thousands, probably millions of human hours that went into making that happen.
So I agree with you.
Yeah.
And when you see it for yourself, it's, it's emotional, especially when you see a solar array turning and you know, there's a Spartan at the
console monitoring that or a CMG that's spinning and the ad co that's sitting on console is like looking at Torx.
I mean, every, every bit of the space station, there is somebody, um, somebody in the front room and the back room and across the world
that's got a part in, in its daily operation.
And you're looking at it and you wish they could see what you could see.
It's like I said, it's emotional.
It's a Marvel.
Right.
That's a great word.
Yeah, it's a Marvel.
And you also have a perspective that not everyone who visits there gets to have because you've done some space walks.
Yeah, that'll yeah, that's a perspective for sure.
And hard to describe.
What's that like going out the hatch and the work that you did, you know?
Well, just going out the hatch itself is, um, a mixture of, um, personal triumph because it's something I think every astronaut wants to do.
And we trained so long and hard for that.
And, um, you're in an environment that's so, um, in, in a training environment that is so, um, as close as you can get to what
you're going to do in space.
But the thing that it cannot replicate or prepare you for is that view.
Once you open up the hatch and you see the planet and the only thing between it and you is this visor covering your face.
And you're just like, this is the coolest thing ever.
And until that happens for the first time, you're really not sure how you're going to handle it.
